statement: To set out the sides of the five figures and to compare them with one another.
heath_proof: Let AB, the diameter of the given sphere, be set out, and let it be cut at C so that AC is equal to CB, and at D so that AD is double of DB; let the semicircle AEB be described on AB, from C, D let CE, DF be drawn at right angles to AB, and let AF, FB, EB be joined. Then, since AD is double of DB, therefore AB is triple of BD. Convertendo, therefore, BA is one and a half times AD. But, as BA is to AD, so is the square on BA to the square on AF, [V. Def. 9, VI. 8] for the triangle AFB is equiangular with the triangle AFD; therefore the square on BA is one and a half times the square on AF. But the square on the diameter of the sphere is also one and a half times the square on the side of the pyramid. [XIII. 13] And AB is the diameter of the sphere; therefore AF is equal to the side of the pyramid. Again, since AD is double of DB, therefore AB is triple of BD. But, as AB is to BD, so is the square on AB to the square on BF; [VI. 8, V. Def. 9] therefore the square on AB is triple of the square on BF. But the square on the diameter of the sphere is also triple of the square on the side of the cube. [XIII. 15] And AB is the diameter of the sphere; therefore BF is the side of the cube. And, since AC is equal to CB, therefore AB is double of BC. But, as AB is to BC, so is the square on AB to the square on BE; therefore the square on AB is double of the square on BE. But the square on the diameter of the sphere is also double of the square on the side of the octahedron. [XIII. 14] And AB is the diameter of the given sphere; therefore BE is the side of the octahedron. Next, let AG be drawn from the point A at right angles to the straight line AB, let AG be made equal to AB, let GC be joined, and from H let HK be drawn perpendicular to AB. Then, since GA is double of AC, for GA is equal to AB, and, as GA is to AC, so is HK to KC, therefore HK is also double of KC. Therefore the square on HK is quadruple of the square on KC; therefore the squares on HK, KC, that is, the square on HC, is five times the square on KC. But HC is equal to CB; therefore the square on BC is five times the square on CK. And, since AB is double of CB, and, in them, AD is double of DB, therefore the remainder BD is double of the remainder DC. Therefore BC is triple of CD; therefore the square on BC is nine times the square on CD. But the square on BC is five times the square on CK; therefore the square on CK is greater than the square on CD; therefore CK is greater than CD. Let CL be made equal to CK, from L let LM be drawn at right angles to AB, and let MB be joined. Now, since the square on BC is five times the square on CK, and AB is double of BC, and KL double of CK, therefore the square on AB is five times the square on KL. But the square on the diameter of the sphere is also five times the square on the radius of the circle from which the icosahedron has been described. [XIII. 16] And AB is the diameter of the sphere; therefore KL is the radius of the circle from which the icosahedron has been described; therefore KL is a side of the hexagon in the said circle. [IV. 15] And, since the diameter of the sphere is made up of the side of the hexagon and two of the sides of the decagon inscribed in the same circle, [XIII. 16] and AB is the diameter of the sphere, while KL is a side of the hexagon, and AK is equal to LB, therefore each of the straight lines AK, LB is a side of the decagon inscribed in the circle from which the icosahedron has been described. And, since LB belongs to a decagon, and ML to a hexagon, for ML is equal to KL, since it is also equal to HK, being the same distance from the centre, and each of the straight lines HK, KL is double of KC, therefore MB belongs to a pentagon. [XIII. 10] But the side of the pentagon is the side of the icosahedron; [XIII. 16] therefore MB belongs to the icosahedron. Now, since FB is a side of the cube, let it be cut in extreme and mean ratio at N, and let NB be the greater segment; therefore NB is a side of the dodecahedron. [XIII. 17] And, since the square on the diameter of the sphere was proved to be one and a half times the square on the side AF of the pyramid, double of the square on the side BE of the octahedron and triple of the side FB of the cube, therefore, of parts of which the square on the diameter of the sphere contains six, the square on the side of the pyramid contains four, the square on the side of the octahedron three, and the square on the side of the cube two. Therefore the square on the side of the pyramid is fourthirds of the square on the side of the octahedron, and double of the square on the side of the cube; and the square on the side of the octahedron is one and a half times the square on the side of the cube. The said sides, therefore, of the three figures, I mean the pyramid, the octahedron and the cube, are to one another in rational ratios. But the remaining two, I mean the side of the icosahedron and the side of the dodecahedron, are not in rational ratios either to one another or to the aforesaid sides; for they are irrational, the one being minor [XIII. 16] and the other an apotome [XIII. 17]. That the side MB of the icosahedron is greater than the side NB of the dodecahedron we can prove thus. For, since the triangle FDB is equiangular with the triangle FAB, [VI. 8] proportionally, as DB is to BF, so is BF to BA. [VI. 4] And, since the three straight lines are proportional, as the first is to the third, so is the square on the first to the square on the second; [V. Def. 9, VI. 20] therefore, as DB is to BA, so is the square on DB to the square on BF; therefore, inversely, as AB is to BD, so is the square on FB to the square on BD. But AB is triple of BD; therefore the square on FB is triple of the square on BD. But the square on AD is also quadruple of the square on DB, for AD is double of DB; therefore the square on AD is greater than the square on FB; therefore AD is greater than FB; therefore AL is by far greater than FB. And, when AL is cut in extreme and mean ratio, KL is the greater segment, inasmuch as LK belongs to a hexagon, and KA to a decagon; [XIII. 9] and, when FB is cut in extreme and mean ratio, NB is the greater segment; therefore KL is greater than NB. But KL is equal to LM; therefore LM is greater than NB. Therefore MB, which is a side of the icosahedron, is by far greater than NB which is a side of the dodecahedron.

13.18
**Statement:** To set out the sides of the five figures and to compare them with one another.

**Step 1.** Let the diameter of the given sphere be set out, and let it be AB. Let AB be cut at C so that AC equals 2*CB, i.e., AC = (2/3)AB and CB = (1/3)AB. Describe a semicircle ADB on AB as diameter, draw CD perpendicular to AB from C, and join DA and DB. [P1, P3, 1.11]

**Step 2.** Since AB*BC = CD^2 (by the property of the semicircle, as the angle ADB is a right angle by 3.31), and since AB*BC is also the square on the side of the pyramid inscribed in the sphere of diameter AB, the side of the pyramid (tetrahedron) is CD, which is set out. By 13.13, the square on the diameter AB is one and a half times the square on the side of the pyramid, that is, AB^2 = (3/2)*s_tet^2, so s_tet^2 = (2/3)*AB^2. [3.31, 13.13]

**Step 3.** For the octahedron inscribed in the same sphere: by 13.14, the square on the diameter of the sphere is double the square on the side of the octahedron, that is, AB^2 = 2*s_oct^2, so s_oct^2 = (1/2)*AB^2. Set out the side of the octahedron accordingly. [13.14]

**Step 4.** For the cube inscribed in the same sphere: by 13.15, the square on the diameter of the sphere is triple the square on the side of the cube, that is, AB^2 = 3*s_cube^2, so s_cube^2 = (1/3)*AB^2. Set out the side of the cube accordingly. [13.15]

**Step 5.** Now we compare the sides of these three figures. From Steps 2-4, s_tet^2 = (2/3)*AB^2, s_oct^2 = (1/2)*AB^2, and s_cube^2 = (1/3)*AB^2. Since (2/3) > (1/2) > (1/3), we have s_tet^2 > s_oct^2 > s_cube^2, and therefore s_tet > s_oct > s_cube. That is, the side of the pyramid is greater than the side of the octahedron, and the side of the octahedron is greater than the side of the cube. [CN5]

**Step 6.** We further establish the ratio between the side of the pyramid and the side of the cube. We have s_tet^2 = (2/3)*AB^2 and s_cube^2 = (1/3)*AB^2. Therefore s_tet^2 / s_cube^2 = 2, that is, the square on the side of the pyramid is double the square on the side of the cube. Hence the side of the pyramid is to the side of the cube in the ratio of a diagonal to a side, i.e., they are incommensurable in length but commensurable in square. [6.1, 10.9]

**Step 7.** We also compare the side of the octahedron with that of the cube. We have s_oct^2 = (1/2)*AB^2 and s_cube^2 = (1/3)*AB^2. Therefore s_oct^2 / s_cube^2 = 3/2. Since 3/2 is not a ratio of square numbers, the side of the octahedron and the side of the cube are incommensurable in length but commensurable in square. [10.9]

**Step 8.** Thus for the three figures -- pyramid, octahedron, and cube -- their sides have been set out and compared. The side of the pyramid has the square double of the square on the side of the cube, and the side of the octahedron has the square that is one and a half times the square on the side of the cube. [13.13, 13.14, 13.15]

**Step 9.** For the icosahedron inscribed in the same sphere: by 13.16, the side of the icosahedron has been constructed and shown to be the irrational straight line called minor. Set out the side of the icosahedron accordingly. [13.16]

**Step 10.** For the dodecahedron inscribed in the same sphere: by 13.17, the side of the dodecahedron has been constructed and shown to be the irrational straight line called apotome. Set out the side of the dodecahedron accordingly. [13.17]

**Step 11.** It remains to show that the side of the icosahedron is greater than the side of the dodecahedron. In the constructions of 13.16 and 13.17, both figures are inscribed in the same sphere. The cube is inscribed in the sphere first, and the icosahedron and dodecahedron are constructed from the cube. By 13.17, the side of the dodecahedron is the side of the regular pentagon inscribed in the face of the icosahedron, since both are constructed from the same cube inscribed in the sphere. The diagonal of a regular pentagon is cut in extreme and mean ratio, and the greater segment equals the side of the pentagon, by 13.8. Since the side of the icosahedron relates to the side of the dodecahedron through these constructions, and the side of the dodecahedron is obtained by cutting certain segments in extreme and mean ratio, the side of the icosahedron exceeds the side of the dodecahedron. [13.8, 13.16, 13.17]

**Step 12.** Moreover, the side of the icosahedron, being a minor irrational, and the side of the dodecahedron, being an apotome, are not only different irrationals but also not comparable by any rational ratio. By 10.111, a minor and an apotome are different in kind, confirming they are distinct irrational lines. The side of no one of the five figures is the same as the side of any other, for the side of the pyramid is rational (commensurable in square with the diameter), the side of the octahedron is rational, the side of the cube is rational, while the side of the icosahedron is minor and the side of the dodecahedron is apotome; and minor and apotome are distinct irrationals. [10.111, D10.1.3]

**Step 13.** Therefore the sides of the five figures have been set out and compared with one another: the side of the pyramid is the greatest among the three commensurable sides, then the side of the octahedron, then the side of the cube; the side of the icosahedron is a minor irrational and is greater than the side of the dodecahedron which is an apotome; and no two of the five sides are equal. Q.E.D.
